basis: 28 reels listed with views, out of 2,252 posts (3 pinned, 1 posted minutes before the look). Covers read for 25. Caption and counters read for 9. Still frames for 2. Spoken words read for 7 (the 3 pinned reels and the 4 recent hits) from the desktop app's transcripts on 20 Nov; no ordinary or low reel has a transcript yet, so the transcripts show what the big reels say, not what separates them from the rest. Views are not adjusted for a reel's age. Groups hold 2 to 9 reels. Comments were not read. Every reading below is a lead to test, not a rule.

works.title: A task with a return date
works.numbers: Six reels give the viewer something to do and a time to come back. Three sit near 300K, like the rest of the page. Three reached 923K, 1.0M and 1.7M: that is 3 of the 4 recent reels at 3x the median or more.
works.reading: Views: unchanged. When this page spikes, it is usually this kind, though three of the six sit at the page's normal level. Comments: WEAKENED by the transcripts. All 3 hits tell the viewer out loud to comment something: two say to comment a keyword to get details of her paid programme, and the biggest tells the viewer to comment the time they are watching and calls that a 'seal'. Only one of the three (the 24-hour test) asks the viewer to come back and say what happened. The 4 skits read closely have no spoken ask at all. So the comment gap (0.4% to 2.5% against 0.02% to 0.05%) is explained at least as well by a direct 'comment this' as by the return date. 'A plain version reached about 1M': WEAKENED. The 24-hour test asks the Universe for a gift within 24 hours and ends on a paid pitch; the 11:11 reel is a money ritual tied to a calendar date in the week it was posted, also ending on a paid pitch. Neither uses secrecy, but neither is a bare task plus date. The biggest (1.7M) stacks things we would not use: secrecy, 'seeing this is a sign', a prediction for the next 7 days, send it to yourself, and the comment 'seal'. The return in 7 days is a small part of it. Not known: what the three ordinary task reels (252K, 301K, 311K) say. Without them nothing here shows why a task reel does or does not spike.

works.title: The Universe as a character
works.numbers: 9 of 28 reels are a two-role "POV" skit. Median 328K, close to the page's 304K. One is pinned at 8.3M and one recent reached 1.3M.
works.reading: This is the page's house format: quick to repeat, recognisable at once, steady. It holds the middle; it is not where most of the recent spikes came from. Transcripts (2 skits only, both big ones: pinned 8.3M and 1.3M): both start inside the scene with the wish addressed to the character by name, no greeting; the character answers within about 4 seconds in a way the asker does not expect (a refusal in one, a 'granted' that goes wrong in the other); the asker protests; the character hands the responsibility back to the asker; the last line is a turn. Neither has any spoken ask; follow is asked only in the caption. No ordinary or low skit has a transcript, so this is how her big skits are built, not proof of why they were big.

weak.title: Bold claims to a mic
weak.numbers: "Lazy people manifest faster" 248K, "Your ex is the reason" 271K, "5 rules" 341K. Median of the group 260K, under the page's 304K. The same set-up is pinned at 12.3M.
weak.reading: Lowest group among the recent reels. Their captions were not read, so the reason is not known.

weak.title: Some skits fall well below the others
weak.numbers: "Where is my soft life?" 160K, "Nobody believes in me" 177K, "I want a million dollars" 186K.
weak.reading: Not explained by the cover: "I want a million dollars" sits at 186K while the very similar "I asked for MORE money" reached 1.3M. The one low skit read closely has the lowest share rate seen, 0.57% of views against 1.4% to 4.6% in the other eight. STILL NOT KNOWN after the transcripts: only the 1.3M skit was transcribed, not the 186K one or any other low skit. The low ones are in the next batch.

weak.title: Part 2 of a list
weak.reading: Two reels only. The sequel reached fewer people than the first.

combine.title: One concept the pieces add up to
combine.text: A named character answers the viewer's wish (the skit), sets a small task with a deadline (the task reels), and the viewer comes back. Her reels use one or two of these parts; none of the ones looked at uses all three. Corrected by the transcripts: 'the viewer reports back in comments' is asked for in only 1 of the 3 task hits; the other two ask for a keyword comment or a time-stamp comment. What people actually wrote is not known (comments not read).
combine.for_us: Tarot Talk's 2027 series already has the character (the saarthi who drives your year). Add the task and the date: find your driver number, comment it, come back on 1 January.

growing.text: Not known yet. Views were read three times within about 16 minutes, which only shows the newest reels still moving. A reel that keeps growing weeks later can only be seen by reading the page again on other days.
growing.next: Read the reels grid once a day for a week. The dashboard will then show which reels are still gaining.

best.why: Best seen among the 28 listed, and pinned by her. A guaranteed-outcome hook on money in the first 3 seconds, then a say-these-lines script for 60 seconds at bedtime. Corrected by the transcript: the '60 seconds' is the length of the bedtime practice, not of the reel, and nothing is sold in the spoken reel. The offer (an 11-day paid programme, comment a keyword) sits only in the caption. The reel is dated 24 June and the caption describes a November programme, so the caption was most likely rewritten later; when is not known.

Pinned by her. The house skit, with pain as the wish. 108 seconds, the longest reel read. Transcript: one picture (a knife held in the asker's own hand) carried through the whole reel; the character refuses in the second line; the asker ends up naming their own reasons for holding on. No spoken ask.

Pinned by her. A "signs you are..." list with a hold-back on the cover ("esp the last one"). The only list of this kind among the 28 seen. Transcript: three signs only, each a broad flattering description many people would recognise in themselves; the hold-back is on the cover, not spoken; it ends on the third sign with no spoken ask.

Best of the recent reels. Opens on a secrecy hook. Corrected by the transcript: not three asks but five, all spoken: hold a fist until the end, send it to yourself, save it, comment the exact time, and come back. Saving and commenting are named as 'seals'. It also tells the viewer that seeing it is a sign and predicts a change within 7 days. 42.1K comments by the script's count, after a spoken instruction to comment.

shapes.name: Two-role skit
shapes.structure: One fixed line on screen for the whole reel naming the wish. Role A asks. Role B, a named character, answers with a twist. Captions on every line.
shapes.ours: Fixed line: "Mulank same. Saal alag?" Passenger asks why this year feels different; the saarthi answers.

shapes.name: The timed promise
shapes.structure: Hook names a length of time and a result. Corrected by the transcript: on her reel the time is how long a bedtime practice takes and the result is a guaranteed outcome, not something the viewer will know by the end of the reel.
shapes.ours: "60 second mein jaaniye, aapka 2027 kaun chala raha hai." Our version promises knowledge inside the reel, never an outcome; that is our change, not her shape. On this page a clock in the hook gave mixed results.

shapes.name: Test it and report back
shapes.structure: One small thing to try, a deadline, and an invitation to come back and say what happened. Transcript: the thing to try is a short set of lines to say aloud, the return ask is spoken once near the end and repeated in the caption, and the last 8 seconds are a paid pitch with a comment keyword. Her version asks for a 'gift' as proof within 24 hours, which we would not copy.
shapes.ours: "Aaj apna driver number nikaaliye. Kal bataiye, kya yeh aapke saal jaisa lagta hai?"

shapes.name: Do / don't columns
shapes.structure: Two columns on screen, ticks and crosses, one pair per beat.
shapes.ours: "Driver 7 ka saal: yeh kijiye / yeh mat kijiye." One driver per reel, or one theme with all nine.

shapes.name: The date anchor
shapes.structure: A practice tied to one calendar moment. Transcript: the steps are physical (write a number, hold a glass, repeat a line three times, keep the paper in the wallet) and the spoken return date is one year later (open the paper). 'Save and come back' is in the caption only. The last 7 seconds are a paid pitch with a comment keyword.
shapes.ours: 31 December closing and 1 January opening. Keep it a reflection, not a ritual that "must" be done.

shapes.name: "This video found you"
shapes.from: "The Universe shows you this video 12 hours before it happens"
shapes.structure: Tells the viewer that seeing the reel is itself a sign or a prediction.
shapes.ours: Do not use. It is a false prophecy: the reel reaches people by the feed, not by fate. Second-highest group here (median 499K, 2 reels), which is exactly why it needs a clear no.

shapes.name: "Send it to yourself"
shapes.structure: Asks the viewer to share the reel to their own chat as part of a ritual. Transcript: spoken at 37 seconds, with the reason given that the viewer will see a change on coming back.
shapes.ours: Do not use. It raises the share counter without anyone recommending the reel. Ask for a real send instead: "apne same-mulank dost ko bhejiye".

shapes.name: Secrecy and pressure hooks
shapes.from: "Don't tell anyone", "Don't fall asleep without saying this", "never be poor again"
shapes.structure: Secrecy, a threat of missing out, or a guaranteed result. Transcript: the 1.7M reel adds two more of the same family, a comment and a save renamed as 'seals', and a physical hold (a fist) kept until the end of the reel.
shapes.ours: Do not use. These break Tarot Talk's honesty rules: no fear, no guaranteed outcome.

shapes.name: Do it along with the reel
shapes.from: 4 of the 7 reels transcribed (the 12.3M pinned reel and the three task hits)
shapes.structure: The reel is a script for the viewer to carry out: lines to say aloud, something to write, something to hold. The speaker gives the words slowly so they can be repeated.
shapes.ours: "Apni janm tithi likhiye. Din aur mahina jodiye, phir 2027 jodiye." The viewer works out their own number while the reel runs. A calculation, never a ritual with a promised result. Seen only in reels picked because they were big, so nothing shows it causes views.

shapes.name: Free practice, pitch in the last seconds
shapes.from: The 24-hour test (last 8 of 39 seconds) and the 11:11 reel (last 7 of 76 seconds)
shapes.structure: The reel is complete without the product. The pitch comes after the practice is finished, starts with a passing 'by the way' kind of line, and asks for one comment keyword. The same keyword is used across reels and captions.
shapes.ours: This is our own reel to keyword to DM path, with the keyword spoken at the very end. Her line about how many people have joined is her own claim; we would state only numbers we can show.

notproven.title: "Money topics do better"
notproven.numbers: 10 of the 25 covers read are about money, so it is her main subject. By cover labels the money reels that are not pinned have a median of 303K against 306K for the rest (328K if the 3 unread covers are left out). CORRECTED by the transcripts: '3 of the 4 recent hits are not about money' was wrong. The 11:11 reel (1.0M) is a money ritual from start to finish, which its cover did not show; the 1.3M skit is about income; the 1.7M reel promises money among other things; the 24-hour test ends on a pitch for a money programme. So 2 of the 4 recent hits are money reels and the other two touch money. With the 11:11 reel moved to money: 307K (9 reels) against 301K (15 reels).
notproven.reading: Still common, not shown to be stronger: the medians are level either way. But the old argument against it (hits are mostly not money) no longer holds, and cover labels can miss the subject. Not proven in either direction.

notproven.title: "A clock in the hook does better"
notproven.numbers: Hooks that name a time: 12.3M (pinned), 1.0M, 923K, 691K, but also 311K, 301K and 252K.
notproven.reading: Mixed. Some of her best and some of her ordinary reels use it.

transcript_study.limits: All 7 were chosen because they are pinned or hits. A transcript shows what was said, not why a reel did well. Words on screen, pictures and comments are not in a transcript. Independent review: NOT DONE in this run (the research agent had no tool to start a reviewer).
transcript_study.hooks: In all 7 the whole premise is spoken within the first 3.5 seconds, with no greeting, name or introduction. Seven different kinds: a guaranteed result, a list label, a plea in character, a wish in character, an offer of proof, secrecy, a calendar claim. So no single hook type is shared; what is shared is that nothing comes before the premise.
transcript_study.pace: Speech is nearly continuous: the script found no pause of note in 5 of 7 reels and three short ones in the longest. Loudness is level across all 7 (average -16.5 to -17.5 dB).
transcript_study.asks: Spoken ask present in 3 of 7 (the three task hits), absent in 4 of 7 (both skits, the list, the 12.3M pinned reel). Two of the three spoken asks are a paid pitch with the keyword 1111. Captions carry the rest: follow, save, send to someone, a note that the account is safe to follow (2 pinned reels), or the offer.
transcript_study.return_dates: 24-hour test: come back tomorrow (spoken and caption). 11:11 reel: open the paper one year later (spoken); come back on the date (caption). 1.7M reel: come back, 7 days named in the caption and as the time of a predicted change in speech.

next_batch.why: Every transcript so far is of a big reel. The findings turn on comparisons the transcripts cannot yet make.
